title: CMOS Technology: Where We Are and How We Got Here

questions.q: What did Gordon Moore's 1965 paper, the origin of 'Moore's law', actually describe?
options: An economic trend: the number of components per chip at the lowest cost per component was doubling regularly
A law of physics: transistors become twice as fast every time their size is halved
A rule of thumb: chip performance doubles every 18 months because clocks get faster
A design rule: the supply voltage must halve whenever the transistor count doubles
questions.explain: Moore's paper was about where the cost minimum sits: the number of components per chip at the lowest cost per component. It held for decades because the industry organised its investment to make it hold, not because of physics.

questions.q: True or false: Moore's own prediction was that the number of components per chip would double every 18 months.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. Moore said every year (1965), then every two years (1975). The '18 months' is a later paraphrase, usually attributed to David House at Intel.

questions.q: Why did Dennard (constant-field) scaling make each new generation a 'free lunch' for about 30 years?
options: Shrinking dimensions and voltages together gave more, faster transistors while the chip got no hotter
Shrinking the transistors kept the voltages the same, so each new chip ran at twice the old supply
Every new generation used a new semiconductor material, which made the transistors faster
Each shrink halved the cost of a wafer, so chips got cheaper even without any gain in speed
questions.explain: Divide every dimension, the supply voltage and the threshold voltage by the same factor: you get more transistors, each faster, at the same power density. Nothing new had to be invented; the same design was printed smaller.

questions.q: Why could the threshold voltage V_T not keep falling after the early 2000s?
options: Below threshold the current can fall no faster than ten times per 60 mV, so each 60 mV off V_T raises leakage tenfold
A lower V_T raises the field across the gate oxide, so gate tunnelling grows tenfold for every 60 mV removed
A lower V_T needs heavier channel doping, so the junctions break down at the supply voltage
A lower V_T makes the carriers saturate their velocity, so the drive current stops rising
questions.explain: The subthreshold slope is at best 60 mV per decade at room temperature. Lowering V_T by 60 mV raises every transistor's off-current tenfold, and with 10⁸ transistors per chip the leakage power became as large as the switching power.

questions.q: The graph shows the maximum clock frequency of processors over the years. What happened around 2004, and where did the extra transistors go after that?
questions.alt: Clock frequency on a log scale rising steeply from 1970 to about 4 GHz around 2004, then almost flat; a dashed line marks the end of Dennard scaling
options: Clock frequency stopped rising near 4 GHz; the extra transistors went into parallelism such as multicore chips and GPUs
Clock frequency started rising twice as fast; the extra transistors went into longer and faster pipelines
Clock frequency fell back to 1 GHz; the extra transistors went into larger caches to hide the slower clock
Clock frequency kept rising steadily; the extra transistors went into more memory on the same chip
questions.explain: When the supply voltage stopped scaling, power density limited the clock to about 4 GHz. Since then the extra transistors have gone into parallelism: multicore processors (2005), GPUs and AI accelerators.

questions.q: Why did chipmakers replace the SiO₂ gate insulator with a high-k material around 2007?
options: At about 1 nm, electrons tunnelled through SiO₂; high-k gives the same capacitance in a thicker film
SiO₂ trapped too much charge at its interface; high-k films hold the threshold voltage steadier
SiO₂ could not be etched finely enough; high-k films can be patterned to smaller sizes
SiO₂ slowed the electrons in the channel; high-k films raise the carrier mobility
questions.explain: By the 90 nm generation the SiO₂ was only about 1 nm thick and electrons tunnelled straight through it. A hafnium-based film with k ≈ 20–25 gives the same gate capacitance at four to five times the thickness, with far less leakage.

questions.q: Strained silicon carries current faster than unstrained silicon. What is the main reason?
options: Strain changes the shape of the bands, giving carriers a lighter effective mass and fewer scattering events
Strain makes the band gap much smaller, so more carriers are available to carry the current
Strain adds extra dopant atoms to the channel, so there are more carriers to carry the current
Strain makes the silicon thinner, so the gate controls the channel more strongly
questions.explain: Strain warps the bands: carriers get a lighter transport mass and scatter less between valleys, so mobility rises. The band gap does change a little, but that is not the mechanism, although it is often stated as if it were.

questions.q: By the 22 nm generation (2011), what problem did the FinFET solve by wrapping the gate around a fin?
options: The drain was competing with the gate for control of the channel; gating from three sides restored the gate's control
The gate oxide was leaking by tunnelling; the fin made the oxide thicker and so stopped the leakage
The wires between transistors were too long; the fin let the transistors sit closer to the wires
The silicon wafers were too small; the fin let each wafer hold twice as many transistors
questions.explain: The problem was electrostatic control: in a short planar transistor the drain competes with the gate. Gating the fin from three sides carried logic from 22 nm down to 3 nm.

questions.q: What does a gate-all-around nanosheet transistor (2 nm class, 2025) offer over a FinFET?
options: The gate surrounds the channel on all four sides, and the channel width is set by the sheet rather than in whole fins
The channel is made of carbon nanotubes instead of silicon, so the electrons move much faster than in a fin
The gate is placed underneath the wafer, so the wiring above has more room for signals
The nMOS transistor sits on top of the pMOS transistor, so each logic cell takes half the area
questions.explain: In a nanosheet the gate encloses each sheet on all four sides, and the width is chosen by the sheet width rather than in whole fins. (Power under the wafer is backside power; stacked nMOS on pMOS is the CFET.)

questions.q: The chart compares three '2 nm' processes. What does the '2 nm' in the name actually measure?
questions.alt: Bar chart for TSMC N2, Intel 18A and Samsung SF2: contacted gate pitch 48–50 nm, tightest metal pitch 26–32 nm, and the number in the node name about 2
options: Nothing physical: it is a generation label, while the real gate pitch is about 48–50 nm
The length of the gate, which is 2 nm in all three processes
The distance between two neighbouring fins, which is 2 nm in all three processes
The thickness of the gate oxide, which is 2 nm in all three processes
questions.explain: Node names were once a real dimension; now they are generation labels. The 2 nm processes have gate pitches of 48–50 nm, metal pitches of 26–32 nm and a physical gate length of about 12 nm.
